messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Sampling 3 areas (regions) during 3 years
messages.body_plain:
Helena

Welcome to the list. My suggestion would be to treat each area/year combination as a stratum, resulting in nine strata in your data. You can then produce stratum-specific density estimates.

However, you should not assume that detectability is the same for all areas in all years. You would build a detection function model where detectability is constant across strata and a different detection function model where detectability differs between strata (fit a separate detection function for each stratum).  You will then use model selection techniques to assess which model is best for your data.

Examples of such analyses with strata are provided
here <https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-strata/strata-distill.html> using R and
here <https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/> using Distance for Windows.
Chapter 5 Stratification, clusters and covariates <https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/syllabus/Chapter5/>
Teaching distance sampling through video lectures and computer exercises.
workshops.distancesampling.org <http://workshops.distancesampling.org>

You can write to me privately if you have further questions.

messages.body_plain:
Interactive introductory distance sampling training

The University of St Andrews has been training ecologists and statisticians in design and analysis of distance sampling studies for decades. Distance sampling methods are widely used in population assessment of many different taxonomic groups. Perhaps you've wanted to attend a previous workshop, but schedules conflicted with your field work. 👨‍🌾

We are offering the training workshop in 10 2.5-hour blocks in October 2024.  You will be invited to interact in short lectures on distance sampling principles. 👩‍🎓 Exercises analysing data sets in R will reinforce those principles and the lecturer will be available to assist during the practical session via screen sharing.  The session will conclude with a summary of the exercise and question/answer session for both lecture and exercise. 💻  You can participate in polls during the workshop to assess your comprehension of topics discussed. 🤔 In addition to questions at any time during the lectures and practicals, an optional additional half hour will be set aside each session for discussion of topics arising. 🗣

New for October 2024: Simultaneous translation of lectures and discussions will be available in closed captions courtesy of Zoom. If English is not your first language, translation will be available into (most) languages. Contact instructor for more details.

The workshop will be delivered using Zoom web conferencing software along with R-Studio "in the cloud".☁️ You will need (free) accounts for both pieces of software. I encourage you to experiment with Zoom (at  https://zoom.us) and  https://posit.cloud before the workshop begins. 👩‍💻  There will be an internet connection testing and general orientation session the week of 23 September 2024.

Important details
Workshop dates and time:  07-18 October 2024; 1400-1630 British Standard Time.
For the time of day in your time zone, consult  this time-keeping site <https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/fixedtime.html?msg=Introductory+distance+sampling+training+workshop&iso=20241007T14&p1=3853&ah=2&am=30>🕰️

www.timeanddate.com <http://www.timeanddate.com>

Enrolment limit: 14
Cost: 225 British pounds 💵
What is included: Lectures, exercises, code, data all available online📃
Widening participation scholarship

One place will have the registration fee waived, for participants from under-represented groups.  Details of eligibility and application process at  http://workshops.distancesampling.org/widening-participation. Deadline for  scholarship application for the October 2024 introductory workshop is 22 July 2024.

The only thing I can say about this particular workshop is it deserves more time. -- Kaan Özgencil, PhD student, Department of Biological Sciences, Middle East Technical University, Ankara

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/intro-oct-2024.html

messages.subject: point count with high variance
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am a biologist working on an Air Force base on Guam. We recently did point count surveys on base for a locally listed bird, Micronesian starling. We have 65 count stations using variable circular plot (5 minute counts) methodology.. For 64 stations our detections were 0-11birds. Sixteen stations had zero. However one station had 28 birds. They are not a flocking species but will live in family groups, but this one spot  has a couple of trees, that appear to be a popular "hang out" spot.

So, this station has caused really wide confidence intervals. With transect lines one can post stratify with overlapping lines to reduce variance. Can we do something similar with point counts? would dropping this station from the analyses be a viable option (I'm guessing the answer is no but had to ask)?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Scott

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] point count with high variance
messages.body_plain:
Greetings Scott; I remember your participation at a workshop in St Andrews some years ago.

Understandably, the encounter rate variance will increase because of the station with the large number of detections. Removal of that station from the data set is not a good idea and you guessed.

The post-stratification tool you describe can be used if the design of the survey used a systematic design. The challenge associated with a systematic design is that an encounter rate variance formula is employed that assumes random transect placement. Usually that approximation is fine, but under some circumstances (an animal gradient compounded by differing transect lengths) this approximation is poor.

The post-stratification technique is not intended to reduce the estimated encounter rate variance; in fact, under many simulated scenarios the technique does not reduce estimated encounter rate variance compared to the usual formula. What I mean is the post-stratification technique is not a panacea; it is intended to address a particular situation.

That said, slides 9-12 of the variance estimation lecture in our online materials discussed how to perform post-stratification for point transect surveys

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch5/L5-1%20Variance%20Estimation%20for%20Systematic%20Designs.pdf

The second portion of the exercise on post-stratification shows that post-stratification does not have the desired effect upon encounter rate variance under "normal" conditions:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/exercisepdfs/Ch5/E5.1%20systematic%20variance%20estimation%20SOLUTION.pdf

Hope that is helpful.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] point count with high variance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,

Thinking about your situation, I've nothing very substantial to add to Eric's advice, especially the detail on post stratification which he knows way more about than me. But I just wanted to make a more general point that in your situation, where you have a modest sample size c and one count that is much higher than the rest, a wide confidence interval around your estimate sounds entirely appropriate. You have one large count out of 48 non-zero counts. If you had 500 more counts, you might get 10 more such large counts, but equally you might get 40, or you might get none. Those different scenarios are completely plausible, and have very different implications for your population estimate. So the wide confidence interval is a fair reflection of your data.

If further data collection is on the cards, some mix of acoustic and traditional monitoring (with overlap to allow calibration). I am not familiar with this species, but if they are like other starlings I guess they make lots of distinctive noise, lending themselves to automated detection and classification using BirdNET (I guess, being a US dependency, Guam might be well served by BirdNET). And if the kind of large family parties you encountered move around, the temporal resolution you can get from a multi month deployment of acoustic recorders could be very useful in helping you understand frequency of occurrence of large groups (assuming you can find a correspondence between large groups and vocalisation rate). Might not be feasible depending on circumstance, but maybe worth considering otherwise.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] point count with high variance
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Eric and Mark, this helps quite a bit.

Yes, I took the course in 2014. If you remember, I was with a Japanese biologist, who is probably one of the few in Japan who can do distance sampling.

Understood that this might not be the end all be all might not be any better than stratifying by region. The stations are systematic and I can stratify by region and have done that and also without stratification. I will try the post-stratification overlap and see what that does. Many thanks for the link to the detailed instructions on that.

Acoustic type surveys would probably be worthwhile but we don't have a budget for that and these surveys are in an urban developed area with lots of backround noise (e.g. fighter jets). It's an interesting situation. You might have heard about brown treesnakes on Guam? A non-native arboreal nocturnal bird eating specialist on a whole island of birds that did not evolve with such a thing. The snake was accidentally transported to Guam during or just after WWII. So the micronesian starling is the only native forest bird left on Guam. It's a cavity nester and this remnant population (it exists in large numbers on other islands in the chain) nests in the buildings in the base housing area where there is snake trapping and base buildings and forages in the forest during the day. We had a project the put out nesting boxes to mounted on power poles that snakes could not access. we'd like to monitor the population and I think distance point counts might be the way to go. This project also did telemetry and survival rates.

Thank you for all of the help!

Scott
